overview: The exact atlas id “nepal-1650” covers 1650 to 1700, but its broad western hill polygon is not modern Nepal and is not one Malla kingdom. It includes tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Lo Manthang, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini while excluding Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, and Banepa. Those excluded Valley cities were three rival kingdoms whose courts drew wealth from farming, crafts, coinage, and India-Tibet trade. Farther west, Gorkha and shifting Baisi and Chaubisi states had their own rulers, alliances, communities, and frontiers. Pratap Malla, Srinivasa Malla, Jagat Prakash Malla, Jitamitra Malla, and Bhupatindra Malla sponsored buildings, manuscripts, festivals, music, and performance while also bargaining, blockading, fighting, taxing, and commanding labor. Surviving records favor kings, priests, donors, and merchants. Farmers, porters, artisans, dependent workers, women, and children appear unevenly, so later customs cannot simply be projected backward. A 1670 multilingual pond inscription provides a rare secure writing sample. At 1700 the atlas erases the target and recolors every tested member point as Mughal Empire. That is a false political ending: neither the Valley kingdoms nor western hill states were annexed by the Mughals then.

periods.title: 1650 to 1654: one polygon, many polities
periods.summary: The atlas creates a western hill “Nepal” feature while leaving all three Valley capitals outside it. In history, Kathmandu secured major Tibet trade and minting privileges around 1650, Patan cultivated western links, and Bhaktapur remained a rival court. The polygon is an editorial aggregate, not their shared frontier.

periods.title: 1654 to 1659: rivalry closes and reopens roads
periods.summary: Pratap Malla's Kathmandu, Srinivasa's Patan, and Jagat Prakash's Bhaktapur maneuvered through blockade, alliance, and attack. In 1658 Patan and Bhaktapur attacked Kathmandu and reopened a route; Pratap then won Srinivasa to his side. Commercial roads were political weapons, and ordinary carriers, market sellers, and neighboring households bore the disruption.

periods.title: 1659 to 1661: Changu violence and a coronation
periods.summary: In 1660 Bhaktapur forces burned a settlement at Changu; the research series records eight people killed and twenty-one captured. Kathmandu and Patan then advanced together. In 1661 Srinivasa was crowned at Patan after years of shared rule, showing how warfare, commerce, local suffering, and dynastic transition overlapped.

periods.title: 1661 to 1666: courts compete through objects and rites
periods.summary: Separate rulers continued to issue coins and sponsor learned and ritual production. Painted manuscript covers commissioned by Srinivasa portray a king, Brahman priest, deities, and royal elephants. Such objects reveal collaborative court workshops and devotional claims, not the furnishings, education, resources, or beliefs of every household.

periods.title: 1666 to 1670: water, words, and royal display
periods.summary: Pratap Malla's Rani Pokhari project culminated in a 1670 inscription beside a rectangular pond and central Shaiva temple. Rubbed and photographed stones preserve Sanskrit, Middle Nepali, and Newari material and name sacred water sources. The monument combined water engineering, ritual geography, public writing, and kingship.

periods.title: 1670 to 1674: monuments and court succession
periods.summary: The 1670 inscription anchors multilingual writing before Gorkha conquest. Pratap Malla died in 1674, while Jagat Prakash's death brought Jitamitra to Bhaktapur in 1673. Court transitions did not end farming, markets, craft work, or festivals, but they could redirect taxes, patronage, alliances, and military risk.

periods.title: 1674 to 1680: Jitamitra and changing Valley balances
periods.summary: Jitamitra ruled Bhaktapur as an architectural patron while Kathmandu and Patan passed through their own successions. A 1678 Patan record still names Srinivasa. The documented reign and inscription dates survive far better than harvests, wages, births, children's routines, or ordinary household disputes from the same years.

periods.title: 1680 to 1685: Patan prepares another transfer
periods.summary: Srinivasa's documented rule ended with abdication in favor of Yoganarendra in 1685. Inscribed ritual objects and manuscripts show how kingship was imagined through protective deities, Sanskrit formulas, and Newari practice. They illuminate an elite ritual world while leaving most residents' spiritual lives only partly visible.

periods.title: 1685 to 1696: poison, sati, and succession
periods.summary: Late-century successions could be violent. Sources report Parthivendra's probable poisoning in 1687 and an inscription saying twenty-four women became sati; another queen survived and sponsored religious works. The evidence warns against romantic tales of willing devotion, assuming consent, or treating elite death rites as every family's experience.

periods.title: 1696 to 1700: Bhupatindra begins, the atlas ends
periods.summary: Bhupatindra succeeded Jitamitra in Bhaktapur in 1696 and continued architectural patronage beyond 1700. The atlas nevertheless deletes nepal-1650 at that date and assigns every tested member point to Mughal Empire. That replacement is a cartographic error, not conquest, collapse, or the disappearance of local communities.

sections.title: Read the atlas label as an aggregate, not a state

items.text: The live index has one exact “nepal-1650” record named “Nepal,” approximately 1650 to 1700. One border file carries it, but the exact card, override, identity review, chronology review, and border review are missing. Its imported summary describes today's country and cannot serve as seventeenth-century copy.

The decoded target is one Polygon with one ring, 33 positions, and bbox 80.10260102601029, 27.27700303211668 to 85.87705877058772, 30.455210042300024. Its geometry hash is d204bc33ad743ae31db7e291ae08f40d66db1cbc0a92c6adb0168b242bc3d037. Coordinates audit the software feature, not a surveyed historical frontier, political census, or legal boundary.

Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Lo Manthang, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini fall inside the target. Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Nepalgunj, Simraungadh, Janakpur, Biratnagar, the Khasa crossing, Shigatse, and Varanasi do not. The shape therefore excludes the best-documented Malla urban core while gathering very different western places.

At 1600 most Valley and central probes carry the catch-all id “islamic-and-hindu-states,” while several western and lowland probes carry “mughal-empire.” At 1650 the new target takes only six tested points. These abrupt assignments reveal atlas generalization; they cannot establish sovereignty, ethnicity, language, or everyday law.

At 1700 and again in 1715, every tested target-member point is colored “mughal-empire.” In 1783 a separate “nepal-1783” shape includes all tested Nepal-related points, including the Valley capitals. The exact target is also distinct from “nepal” and “nepal-1492”; matching names never authorize merged cards, dates, or political stories.

sections.title: Meet three Valley kingdoms and many western states

items.text: Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur were separate city kingdoms, not districts of one seventeenth-century nation. Their Malla courts competed for routes, ritual standing, and political advantage, yet shared a dense Valley world of Newar towns, agriculture, temples, markets, kinship, and craft production. Court borders did not seal daily connections.

West of the Valley, “Baisi” and “Chaubisi” named shifting groupings rather than two tidy federal blocs. The far-western Karnali region included Jumla and other hill states; the Gandaki region included Gorkha, Lamjung, Kaski, Tanahun, and neighbors. Membership and power changed, so lists need dates and caution.

Gorkha, founded as an independent Shah kingdom in 1559, was still one relatively small hill state in this card's period. Its official heritage history describes rivalry with Lamjung, farming as its economic base, forts toward the Trishuli, and relationships with Valley rulers. Later unification should not be read backward into 1650.

Srinivasa's career illustrates divided authority inside a court: he received administrative responsibilities by 1640, shared rule from 1648, was crowned in 1661, and abdicated in 1685. Documenta Nepalica also names parents, spouses, and a son, but a royal genealogy cannot stand in for ordinary family organization.

Jitamitra's 1673 to 1696 Bhaktapur reign and Bhupatindra's succession in 1696 belong to one city kingdom, not the whole polygon. Getty records both as architectural patrons. Buildings may bear royal names while embodying the planning, quarrying, carpentry, brickwork, metalwork, transport, and maintenance of many unnamed workers.

sections.title: Follow diplomacy, war, trade, coins, and revenue

items.text: Around 1650 Kathmandu secured privileged access for its merchants in Lhasa and rights to mint Tibetan coinage from bullion supplied from Tibet. The agreement made commercial opportunity and royal seigniorage inseparable. “Nepal” in later summaries can hide that specific court advantage and the distinct interests of Patan and Bhaktapur.

A Nepal Rastra Bank history links Bhim Malla's mission with duty-free trade and silver coin circulation in Tibet. That account is useful for institutional memory but should not become a story of effortless prosperity. Caravans faced weather, altitude, animals, customs politics, credit risk, and long separation from families.

Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur produced contemporaneous Malla coinages. Coins carried authority and facilitated exchange, but metal content, acceptance, and access mattered. A royal right to mint did not mean every market transaction used silver: produce, labor, credit, and smaller-value media remained central to household economies.

The 1658 to 1660 fighting involved blocked roads, changing alliances, burned property, deaths, prisoners, tribute, and new political claims. Calling these episodes “minor quarrels,” as one older account does, risks minimizing residents' losses. Small wars can still be enormous to the household whose roof, crop, relative, or freedom disappears.

Rulers drew resources from agricultural dues, customs and tolls, land assignments, and labor obligations. Nepal's official customs history traces medieval trade collection, while legal scholarship records slavery and other unfree dependency. Categories and surviving documents vary, but dependent people must not disappear behind cheerful images of caravans and temple building.

sections.title: Work the land, market, road, and workshop

items.text: Irrigated rice and other grains, vegetables, livestock, and seasonal tasks sustained Valley towns; hill ecologies supported different crop mixes and herding. Landholding, tenancy, ritual rank, slope, rainfall, and access to water shaped work. Court-centered sources rarely tell us how one poor harvest redistributed hunger within a family.

Later Newar fieldwork shows households combining farming with pottery, building labor, carrying, shopkeeping, ritual service, or other crafts. It cannot be copied unchanged into 1650. It does help historians ask better questions about seasonal multitasking, small plots, tenancy, and why a single caste label never equals one livelihood.

Kathmandu's Asan market and Uray merchant institutions preserve long commercial histories reaching back into Malla urban life. Merchants needed packers, porters, brokers, lenders, innkeepers, food sellers, translators, and animal handlers. Trade history becomes misleading when it names only kings who negotiated privileges and merchants whose records survived.

Fired brick, carved timber, stone, bronze, terracotta, pigment, cloth, paper, and metal coinage demanded specialized skill and supply chains. UNESCO's monuments demonstrate extraordinary craft, but surviving palaces and temples overweight elite commissions. Everyday pots, repairs, tools, baskets, and work clothes mattered more often to most residents.

Medieval prescriptions tied some occupations, dress, and residence to caste rank, but practice was more varied than a neat chart. Oxford's collaborative study finds distinct priests, patrons, artisans, farmers, merchants, and low castes while stressing internal variation. Treat prescriptive rules as claims about order, not a census of everyone's work.

sections.title: Enter homes, meals, clothes, streets, and social rank

items.text: Malla-period urban blocks used closely built multistory brick-and-timber houses, courtyards, narrow lanes, squares, and monastery compounds. Location and housing reflected wealth, occupation, and caste hierarchy. A courtyard could be kitchen approach, workshop, play space, storage route, and neighborly meeting place, usually without the luxury of doing only one job.

Most families ate from local agricultural cycles rather than palace menus. Rice and other grains mattered in the Valley, while pulses, vegetables, dairy, and meat varied by ecology, means, caste, and religious practice. Agricultural history supports the broad pattern, but any single “Newar diet” would flatten inequality and western communities inside the atlas polygon.

Clothing could signal occupation, gender, status, community, and ritual occasion, yet textiles survive poorly compared with stone temples. Medieval caste rules prescribed dress for some groups, while surviving images show court finery. Neither tells us every child's patched garment or every laborer's weather protection, so ordinary wardrobes remain modestly reconstructed.

Urban morphology linked streets, squares, palace space, temples, shops, and residential quarters, but surviving layouts must not become a perfect caste diagram. Movement through lanes and access to ritual or market centers could express hierarchy. The arrangement reflected social power and changing use, not merely charming traditional zoning.

UNESCO's palace squares and temple ensembles preserve public architecture rather than an average home. Timber roofs, brick walls, carved openings, and courtyards show climatic and craft intelligence, but earthquakes, fire, repair, reuse, and later restoration complicate dating. A beautiful facade is evidence that must still be interrogated.

sections.title: See families, women, children, caste, and coercion

items.text: Families organized care, inheritance, marriage, work, worship, and migration, but no reviewed source supplies one representative 1650 household. Later Newar research identifies joint families, patrilineal kinship, guthi ties, caste, residence, and Hindu-Buddhist coexistence; it is a comparison, not a license to project one pattern across every earlier hill, lowland, rural, or urban family.

Later Newar life-cycle research records girls' ihi rites and considerable variation among communities. It cannot prove that every girl in 1650 followed the same sequence. Use it to explain a living tradition and an evidence limit, never to turn all women or children into timeless performers of one custom.

Sati appears in late-century inscriptions, including reports of women dying after elite men. The documents do not establish free consent, and one research account explicitly considers coercion. These deaths were not a romantic loyalty test. Surviving queens, donors, workers, widows, and women outside courts also prevent one cruel practice from defining womanhood.

Reviewed evidence for children is clearest in ritual scholarship and elite imagery, not daily schedules. Later study of girls' ihi rites cannot reconstruct a 1650 childhood. A painted royal elephant calf beside its mother is court imagery, not proof of schooling. Tiny elephants, sadly, left no homework.

Caste, debt, slavery, compulsory labor, gender, and political rank constrained choice. Legal-historical evidence confirms unfree statuses without yielding a full population count. Human costs belonged to named and unnamed people who carried loads, worked land, served households, built monuments, or were bought, punished, captured, or displaced.

sections.title: Learn languages, manuscripts, education, and a written sample

items.text: Learning happened in courts, Brahman households, Buddhist viharas, ritual lineages, workshops, and merchant families rather than a universal school system. Reading, recitation, account keeping, performance, craft instruction, and manuscript copying demanded different skills. Access depended on status, gender, community, patronage, money, and the purpose of study.

Sanskrit served learned and royal purposes; Newari carried rich local literary and administrative life; Middle Nepali also appears before Gorkha conquest. Maithili and other languages circulated through courts, migration, trade, and performance. The language history defeats any claim that one language uniformly defined this polygon or every resident.

Written-language sample, 1670, Rani Pokhari in Kathmandu: “असल पनाली माथी को देवल”. Transliteration: “asala panālī māthī ko devala.” Published translation: “the temple standing on the asala panālī.” It is a Middle Nepali phrase from a royal pond inscription, presented here in normalized modern Devanagari for readable display.

The sample is not a character-for-character facsimile. “Asala panālī” is a technical place or channel expression left untranslated by the philological source, and spellings vary across transcription. The larger inscription includes Sanskrit and Newari. A royal public text demonstrates multilingual writing, not everyone's spoken sentence.

Srinivasa's painted manuscript covers show patron, priest, sacred book, and deities, while viharas supported copying and learning. These objects required authors, scribes, painters, woodworkers, pigment makers, ritual specialists, and readers. Education history must credit this production network rather than imagining a solitary king writing every page.

sections.title: Join ritual, festival, music, theatre, art, and architecture

items.text: Hindu and Buddhist traditions coexisted with Tantric and local practices across the Valley, often sharing craftsmen, spaces, images, and festivals without becoming identical. Changu Narayan contains Vaishnava, Shaiva, and Shakta significance. Religious plurality involved negotiation and rank as well as the harmonious fusion celebrated by heritage summaries.

Mahanī was embedded in the ritual fabric of distinct Malla city-states. Heidelberg research emphasizes that different royal houses used different specialists and ritual programs. Court worship of Durga supported kingship, but urban participants also made, carried, sang, watched, cleaned, cooked, and organized the festival beyond palace authorship.

Pratap Malla's Sanskrit praise poem on Taleju's golden doors demonstrates literary ambition and royal devotion. The text belongs to a specific court and temple setting. It cannot be generalized as the prayer of every farmer, Buddhist household, western hill community, or low-status worker inside the atlas outline.

Seventeenth-century Malla theatre used raised dabali platforms and could draw kings, courtiers, and wider audiences. Performance joined text, music, dance, costume, carpentry, and public space. Court sponsorship mattered, while actors, musicians, craftspeople, and spectators made the event real. Even royal entertainment required a very nonroyal amount of carrying.

Seventeenth-century terracotta goddesses and late-century Bhaktapur architecture show modeling, firing, carving, masonry, and metal ornament at high levels. Getty names royal patrons but not every maker. The achievement belongs to workshop communities and material knowledge, while restoration and uncertain attribution caution against assigning every surviving surface to one reign.

sections.title: Seek healers, medicines, bodies, and health limits

items.text: People could seek household knowledge, ritual care, plant and mineral remedies, learned Ayurvedic treatment, or practical assistance from specialists, but records favor texts and patrons. Distance, cost, caste, gender, trust, ingredients, and the seriousness of illness shaped access. No source supports one medical system reaching every settlement.

The old Nepalese Susrutasamhita manuscript preserves a learned medical tradition from long before this card's period. Its survival and study show that physicians and scribes could transmit specialized texts. It does not prove that a seventeenth-century child in Jumla could summon a manuscript-trained doctor when a stomachache arrived.

An eighteenth-century Kathmandu manuscript associated with the Bhavaprakasha joined a physician's knowledge with Tibetan artists and calligraphers. It falls just after this card and therefore supplies continuity, not direct 1650 evidence. Its collaborative making nevertheless warns against treating medical knowledge as sealed inside one language or community.

Health depended on food security, clean water, warmth, housing ventilation, workload, pregnancy and birth care, injury, and exposure to people and animals as much as on named remedies. The reviewed court chronicles do not quantify infant mortality, epidemics, disability, or life expectancy for 1650 to 1700. Honest absence beats invented precision.

Manuscript learning and specialist lineages could transmit recipes and procedures, while practical knowledge also moved orally through families and occupations. Viharas and learned households were not public hospitals. A text's presence in the Valley establishes intellectual resources, not equal treatment, reliable dosage, or safe outcomes for every patient.

sections.title: Trace water, drains, waste, toilets, and continuity

items.text: Kathmandu Valley water systems linked rajkulo canals, irrigated fields, ponds, settlement supply, and long-lived community management. The infrastructure predates this card and crossed ruler changes. Users still experienced water through carrying, cleaning, repair, seasonal flow, and negotiated access, not as an abstract engineering diagram.

The Rani Pokhari inscription says water came from numerous sacred sources, and the scholarly edition notes a canal from Sundarijal. The pond and central temple made hydraulic work part of ritual kingship. Sacred water was still moved by channels, vessels, builders, cleaners, and people with very practical muddy feet.

A Bhaktapur institutional case study describes rajkulo supply, stone-spout drainage, wastewater flow, ritual obligations, and guthi maintenance. It draws on later arrangements and cannot automatically date every channel or rule to 1650. The secure conclusion is a layered water tradition whose exact seventeenth-century operation varied by place and repair history.

Later documentation records house sinks, clay wastewater pipes, lanes, drains, and compost pits in Newar settlements. It does not securely inventory seventeenth-century toilets. Therefore this card will not assign one latrine design, wiping material, or waste occupation to all residents. “Evidence missing” is more accurate than a picturesque smell.

The atlas ends the target in 1700 and replaces its sampled footprint with Mughal Empire, but the three Valley kingdoms, Gorkha, Baisi and Chaubisi polities, households, farms, workshops, routes, rituals, and water systems continued. Bhupatindra's reign itself runs beyond the seam. The map changes; these societies do not vanish.

ending.text: At the 1700 atlas seam, “nepal-1650” disappears and all six tested member points move to “mughal-empire,” a replacement that persists in 1715. This was no Mughal annexation or Nepalese collapse. The Valley's three Malla kingdoms and numerous western states continued; a much later and wider “nepal-1783” record reflects a different political era and atlas geometry.
